name: Kisra
subtitle: Kisra is a thin, pancake-like flatbread made from fermented sorghum batter spread on a hot plate.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: In South Sudan, grain flour is most often made into thin pancakes (kisra), porridge ('asida) or couscous (Dinka akob, Nuer kop, Collo akello).

facts.label: Fermentation
facts.value: The flour-and-water batter is often slightly fermented, which makes sorghum proteins more digestible and gives a sour flavour to many South Sudanese dishes.

facts.label: Main ingredient
facts.value: Sorghum, the ancient grain of South Sudan, still provides most of the country's calories.

facts.label: Main ingredient
facts.value: Several hundred sorghum varieties exist in Sudan and South Sudan, some grown only locally.

facts.label: Staple
facts.value: A traditional staple of (pre-2011) Sudan made from sorghum and millet; with Ethiopian injera, one of the main fermented breads made from sorghum flour.

facts.label: How it is cooked
facts.value: A thin pancake bread made by spreading fermented sorghum batter on a hot plate.

facts.label: Household method
facts.value: In the household method, flour is mixed with water in a 1:2 ratio, and 10% starter is added: sourdough kept from a previous kisra fermentation.

facts.label: Fermentation
facts.value: The fermentation is natural, driven by lactic acid bacteria and yeasts.

facts.label: How it is eaten
facts.value: A wafer-thin flatbread of fermented sorghum, thinner than Ethiopian injera, eaten with mulaah, a stew of dried okra.

parts.text: Kisra is a thin, pancake-like flatbread made from fermented sorghum batter spread on a hot plate. In South Sudan, grains are most often milled into flour and made into kisra, porridge ('asida) or a couscous; the batter is usually slightly fermented, which makes sorghum proteins easier to digest and gives a sour taste. Sorghum, grown in the region in hundreds of varieties, still provides most of South Sudan's calories.
It is eaten as a staple bread, for example with mulaah, a stew of dried okra.
